title: Linux.Proxy.10_Incident_Response_Scenario_519
description: Investigate and respond to a Linux.Proxy.10 trojan compromise on a victim host.

levels.title: Introduction
levels.content: The victim host in your network has been compromised by the Linux.Proxy.10 trojan, a malware designed to run a SOCKS5 proxy server on the infected device. This trojan is used by cybercriminals to maintain anonymity online. Your task is to investigate and respond to this incident. You will encounter flags such as service names, timer names, and file paths during this scenario.

levels.title: Get Access
levels.cloud_content:
You have SSH access to the victim host with the following credentials:
- Hostname: victim
- IP Address: 192.168.60.10
- Username: cyrano
- Password: cyrano

To proceed, enter the word 'start' in the input field below.
levels.local_content:
Local sandbox access is not required for this scenario.

To proceed, enter the word 'start' in the input field below.

levels.title: Investigate Suspicious Services
levels.content: Investigate the victim host for any unauthorized or suspicious services running on the system. Enumerate running services and distinguish legitimate services from trojan-related services.
levels.solution: Use `systemctl list-units --type=service` to list all services and `systemctl status <service_name>` to check the status of specific services. The flag you are looking for is the service name 'socks5-proxy'.

hints.title: Conceptual Hint
hints.content: Start by understanding the types of services that might be running on a Linux system.

hints.title: Methodology Hint
hints.content: Enumerate all services to identify any that might be suspicious or unauthorized.

hints.title: Command Hint
hints.content: Use commands like `systemctl list-units --type=service` to list all services and `systemctl status <service_name>` to check the status of specific services. Look for services with names like 'socks5-proxy' that might be related to the malware.

levels.title: Identify Scheduled Task or Timer
levels.content: Determine whether a scheduled task or timer is responsible for automatically executing the malware on the victim host. Identify scheduled execution persistence mechanisms (e.g., cron, systemd timers, Windows Scheduled Tasks).
levels.solution: Use `systemctl list-timers` to list all timers and `systemctl status <timer_name>` to check the status of specific timers. The flag you are looking for is the timer name 'malware-timer'.

hints.title: Conceptual Hint
hints.content: Understand the different types of scheduled tasks and timers that can be used on a Linux system.

hints.title: Methodology Hint
hints.content: Look for timers that might be related to the malware by examining systemd timers and services.

hints.title: Command Hint
hints.content: Use commands like `systemctl list-timers` to list all timers and `systemctl status <timer_name>` to check the status of specific timers. Look for timers with names like 'malware-timer' that might be related to the malware.

levels.title: Locate Malware Files
levels.content: Locate files installed by the malware on the compromised host. Correlate suspicious activity with files introduced by the trojan.
levels.solution: Use `find / -type d -name '.*' 2>/dev/null` to find hidden directories and `find / -type f -name '.*' 2>/dev/null` to find hidden files. The flag you are looking for is the file path '/usr/local/lib/.netd/revshell.sh'.

hints.title: Conceptual Hint
hints.content: Understand that malware often hides files in unusual or hidden directories.

hints.title: Methodology Hint
hints.content: Search for hidden directories and files that might contain malware components or collected data.

hints.title: Command Hint
hints.content: Use commands like `find / -type d -name '.*' 2>/dev/null` to find hidden directories and `find / -type f -name '.*' 2>/dev/null` to find hidden files. Look for files with paths like '/usr/local/lib/.netd/revshell.sh' that might be related to the malware.
